strapline: Copper's worst day since April 2025; ruling day for Mundubile and Zulu; US$105 million for small firms through Zanaco; a crackdown on illicit alcohol; Mkhonta's farewell

stories.title: Copper's worst day since April 2025: a fall of nearly 6 per cent on Wednesday wipes out the metal's November gains and leaves the price close to where the year began
stories.excerpt: Copper lost close to 6 per cent on Wednesday 18 November, its steepest one-day fall since April 2025, before steadying on Thursday, according to bank commentary carried by Zambia Monitor and an analysis by the broker XTB. The metal is down roughly 12 to 13 per cent in November and trades near US$12,560 a tonne, about where it started 2026. For Zambia, whose kwacha slipped to just under K20.50 to the dollar last week, the question is whether September's record highs were the peak.

image.label: Nearly 6% in a day
image.caption: Copper's fall on Wednesday 18 November was its largest single-day decline since April 2025, and November's gains are gone.

body: Copper, Zambia's principal export and the metal to which its currency is most sensitive, had its worst day in more than 18 months on Wednesday 18 November. The price fell by close to 6 per cent before steadying, a move that Zambia Monitor, citing market commentary from Access Bank Group, described on Thursday as the biggest single-day drop since April 2025. The Polish broker XTB, in a note published on Thursday morning by its analyst Michał Jóźwiak, put the fall at nearly 6 per cent and called it the deepest one-day decline since April 2025, the month XTB associates with the US "Liberation Day" tariff shock.

The two accounts agree on the scale of the damage to November. Zambia Monitor's report puts the month's losses at about 12 per cent; XTB says the move since the start of the month has exceeded 13 per cent. Both say the price has given back most of what it gained earlier in the year. XTB quotes a price of about US$5.66 a pound, the lowest in seven months, and a price near US$12,560 a tonne, close to where copper began 2026. Zambia Monitor's report gives no dollar figure, but says the decline has pushed the price back towards the levels recorded at the beginning of the year.

Both commentaries trace the slide to the unwinding of a rally built on two expectations. The first was demand: copper had been bid up on forecasts of heavy buying for data centres, artificial-intelligence infrastructure and grid modernisation, and XTB says doubts about the pace of AI spending, together with regulatory worries after the Democratic victory in this month's US mid-term elections, have cooled that story. The second was tariffs. Zambia Monitor's account says speculation about US duties on refined copper had earlier pulled large volumes of metal into the United States, tightening supply elsewhere and helping to drive the rally to record highs in September; investors are now reassessing demand and reducing bullish positions.

A stronger dollar did the rest. Both accounts cite a repricing of the US Federal Reserve's likely path towards tighter policy, which lifted the dollar and made copper dearer for buyers outside the United States. XTB adds two data points from the week: Chinese industrial production data released on Monday 16 November showed growth of 4.8 per cent year on year, below expectations, while Chile's monthly copper output rose to 388,000 tonnes. Both reports also mention the investor Stanley Druckenmiller, a prominent advocate of the AI-driven copper thesis, who is reported to have turned bearish; XTB says he has disclosed a short position in the metal. Lusaka Brief has not seen that disclosure and reports it as the two outlets do.

body.text: The physical market tells a different story

body: Neither account treats the fall as a collapse in real demand. Zambia Monitor's report says physical market conditions remain relatively tight: inventories in China are described as critically low, and spot copper trades at a significant premium to futures. Among other base metals, aluminium and zinc recovered modestly while tin extended its losses, Zambia Monitor said. XTB's technical reading is that copper is deeply oversold, with its relative strength index below 23 and the price more than 10 per cent under its 50-session moving average, although the longer-term averages still point upwards. The broker's levels to watch are support around US$12,400 a tonne, a further target near US$11,680 if that breaks, and resistance around US$13,360.

The kwacha was already under pressure before the metal turned. Zambia Monitor reported on Monday 16 November that the currency weakened 0.67 per cent in the week to Friday 13 November, closing just below K20.50 to the dollar, its largest weekly decline since the week ending 16 October, as demand for foreign exchange continued to outweigh supply and the dollar traded close to its strongest level since May 2025. The same report said the market was watching for signs that the rise in US Treasury yields was near its limit, which could bring some consolidation in the dollar.

None of the reports read for this story gives a figure for what a lower copper price would mean for Zambia's export earnings, mining royalties or the 2027 Budget, and no statement from the Bank of Zambia, the Ministry of Finance or the Chamber of Mines on Wednesday's fall had been published by Thursday evening in the outlets Lusaka Brief reviewed. Those are the responses to watch, together with Friday's London close, which will show whether Thursday's stabilisation holds.

body.title: The numbers
items: Nearly 6 per cent — copper's fall on Wednesday 18 November, the largest one-day drop since April 2025 (Zambia Monitor, citing Access Bank Group; XTB)
About 12 to 13 per cent — the decline since the start of November (Zambia Monitor; XTB)
About US$12,560 a tonne and US$5.66 a pound — the price XTB quoted on Thursday, the pound price its lowest in seven months
Just under K20.50 — where the kwacha closed against the dollar on Friday 13 November, after a 0.67 per cent weekly loss (Zambia Monitor)
September 2026 — when copper reached record highs, according to Zambia Monitor's account of the rally

body.confirmed: That copper fell by nearly 6 per cent on Wednesday 18 November, its largest one-day fall since April 2025, and has lost about 12 to 13 per cent in November, is reported by Zambia Monitor (citing Access Bank Group commentary) and by XTB. XTB's price levels of about US$12,560 a tonne and US$5.66 a pound are that broker's figures. The kwacha's close just under K20.50 on 13 November is Zambia Monitor's reporting.
body.unverified: Stanley Druckenmiller's reported short position is second-hand in both accounts and Lusaka Brief has not seen the disclosure. The effect on Zambia's export receipts, royalties and the kwacha this week has not yet been reported by any outlet or official body. XTB's support and resistance levels are an analyst's opinion, not a forecast of where the price will go.

stories.title: 09:30 at the High Court: Judge Geoffrey Mulenga rules today on whether Mundubile and Zulu's sedition bail plea can be heard in Lusaka, as Mpika North's MP keeps his seat
stories.excerpt: The Lusaka High Court is due at 09:30 this morning to rule on the Director of Public Prosecutions' objection that Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu's bail application in their sedition case is in the wrong court, the Daily Nation and the Zambian Observer reported on Thursday. A three-judge panel rules on Tuesday 24 November on constitutional bail for all 18 treason accused. Separately, the Daily Nation reports that Judge Catherine Lombe has upheld Francis Kapyanga's election in Mpika North, and that judgment is pending in the Lima petition.

image.label: Friday, 09:30
image.caption: The High Court in Lusaka decides today whether it can hear the sedition bail application brought by Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu.

body: Two rulings in five days will shape the next phase of the cases against Brian Mundubile, the runner-up in August's presidential election, and his running mate Makebi Zulu. The first comes this morning. The Daily Nation reported on Thursday afternoon that the Lusaka High Court is expected to rule today on the bail application the two men have brought in their seditious practices case before Judge Geoffrey Mulenga, and specifically on a preliminary objection by the Director of Public Prosecutions, Gilbert Phiri, that challenges whether the Lusaka High Court has jurisdiction to hear it. The Zambian Observer's morning news brief on Thursday gave the same date, 20 November, for the jurisdictional ruling.

The court reserved that ruling to Friday at 09:30 after hearing argument on Monday 16 November, Zambia Monitor reported that evening. The State's position, as that report describes it, is that the High Court's wide bail powers do not allow a party to bypass transfer procedures; that filing in Lusaka while the sedition matter was still before the Solwezi High Court amounted to a multiplicity of proceedings and an abuse of process; and that, now the case has been transferred to the Lusaka Subordinate Court, the two men should ask that court for bail first. The defence answered that section 123 of the Criminal Procedure Code gives the Lusaka High Court jurisdiction, that the Solwezi magistrate had declined jurisdiction and referred only the question of transfer upwards, and that no bail application had ever been filed in either Solwezi court.

body.text: The charges, and the second ruling

body: The sedition case rests on two counts of seditious practices under section 57 of the Penal Code, arising from Facebook posts and livestreams on 14 August 2026, the day after the general election. According to Zambia Monitor's 16 November report, the first count alleges that Mundubile called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia to announce the winner on the basis of parallel vote tabulation results; the second alleges that Zulu announced that Mundubile would address the nation at a scheduled time. Neither count has been tested at trial. Solwezi High Court Judge Edward Musona ordered the case moved to Lusaka on 5 November, Zambia Monitor reported, because both accused live in the capital and were arrested there.

The second ruling is on Tuesday 24 November, when a panel of three judges, Derrick Mulenga, Davies Chibwili and Ireen Wishimanga, decides the constitutional bail petition brought by Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others held at Mukobeko Maximum Security Correctional Facility in Kabwe since 14 August on treason and related allegations, News Diggers reported on Tuesday. The panel ruled earlier this month that the petition was properly before it, Zambia Monitor reported on 11 November, rejecting a State argument that it should have gone through the criminal registry. In the Diggers report, defence lawyer Sakwiba Sikota described the security arrangements around the treason case as over-dramatised, saying it involved three former commandos; the rest of his remarks sit behind that outlet's subscription.

body.text: Election petitions: Mpika North kept, Lima pending

body: The Daily Nation also reported on Thursday evening, in articles for its subscribers, on two parliamentary election petitions. High Court Judge Catherine Lombe declared Francis Robert Kapyanga the duly elected Member of Parliament for Mpika North, holding that the grounds raised to nullify his election in the 13 August poll did not stand. The identity of the petitioner and the grounds argued are not in the part of the report available to non-subscribers. In a second article, the paper reported that the Lusaka High Court is set to deliver judgment in the Lima constituency petition, in which the losing UPND candidate, Lee Mukupa, challenges the declaration of the NRPUP's Kelvin Kaunda as MP on grounds including alleged violence and intimidation. That petition is before Judge Derrick Mulenga of the Ndola High Court, sitting in Lusaka; the judgment date was not visible in the published extract.

body.confirmed: That the Lusaka High Court is due to rule today, Friday 20 November, on the DPP's jurisdictional objection in the sedition bail application (Daily Nation; Zambian Observer; Zambia Monitor's 16 November report gives 09:30), and on constitutional bail for the 18 on Tuesday 24 November (News Diggers; Zambian Observer). That Judge Catherine Lombe upheld Francis Kapyanga's election in Mpika North is the Daily Nation's report.
body.unverified: The outcome of either ruling. The grounds in the Mpika North petition and the identity of the petitioner, and the date of the Lima judgment, which are behind the Daily Nation's subscription. All charges against Mundubile, Zulu and their co-accused are allegations they deny and which no court has yet tried.

stories.title: 'You can't make law for one man': Kabimba joins the term-limits argument, Harrington says the Speaker should not preside, and Chapter One demands reasons for the march ban
stories.excerpt: Economic Front leader Wynter Kabimba told Prime Television that the law is not made for one man, the Zambian Observer reported on Thursday, as the Daily Nation carried William Harrington's argument that Speaker Nelly Mutti, who sat on the Mung'omba commission that rejected a third term, should recuse herself from any term-limits debate. Chapter One Foundation gave police until Thursday to give specific reasons for advising against the 25 November marches. The Observer also reports Saviour Chishimba's apology for campaigning for the UPND Alliance.

image.label: Article 106(3)
image.caption: The argument over presidential term limits moved on Thursday to who should preside over it and why police advised against two marches.

body: A week before two rival processions are meant to reach Parliament, the argument over presidential term limits turned on Thursday to questions of procedure: who should chair any debate in the National Assembly, and what reasons the police had for advising against the marches. The Zambian Observer's morning brief on Thursday 19 November reported that Wynter Kabimba, leader of the Economic Front, had warned on Prime Television's Matters Arising against changing constitutional rules for one individual. "You can't make law for one man and law is not made for good and bad," he said, in the Observer's account. The same brief, written by The People's Brief news desk and carried by the Observer, quoted a senior UPND official, speaking on condition of anonymity, as saying that even within the ruling party the removal of term limits is a contested matter.

The Daily Nation reported on Thursday evening, in an article for its subscribers, that William Harrington has argued that Nelly Mutti, the Speaker of the National Assembly, should recuse herself from presiding over any debate on the proposed changes. His reason, as the paper summarises it, is that Mutti served on the Mung'omba Constitutional Review Commission, which rejected a third term and the removal of the presidential limit, and that this raises questions about her presiding over proposals to alter the same clause. The Speaker's office has not been reported as responding. The full article is behind the paper's paywall.

body.text: The police letter and the deadline

body: The marches themselves remain in dispute. The police letter of Tuesday 17 November, addressed to Chapter One Foundation's executive director Josiah Kalala and signed by Lusaka Division Commanding Officer Ronald Zambo, cited intelligence information and the prevailing national security situation in advising organisers not to proceed on Wednesday 25 November, the Daily Revelation reported. According to the Observer, civil society groups led by Chapter One challenged the advice, asked for specific reasons and alternative arrangements, requested a written response by Thursday 19 November and said they might pursue legal remedies. The Observer's report did not say whether a reply had been received, and none had been published by Thursday evening in the outlets read for this story.

The Observer and the Daily Revelation both carried a reaction from George Chulumanda, a former minister and ambassador. "This is dictatorship in uniform," he said of the police decision. In the Daily Revelation's account he also asked, "What national security situation? The only security threat in Zambia today is a government that is afraid of term limits," called for the release of Mundubile, Zulu and other detainees he described as political, and urged Zambians to protest peacefully: "Let them arrest 10,000 of us peacefully. Let them fill the prisons with peaceful Zambians." Those are his assertions; neither outlet carried a police or government response to them.

body.text: The government's position, and the view from outside

body: The government's line has not changed. CAJ News Africa, in a report from Lusaka on Thursday, quoted Justice Minister Jack Mwiimbu telling a media conference: "The executive respects the independence of the legislature and will not involve itself in processes". State House, the Observer notes, says President Hakainde Hichilema has no involvement in the campaign to remove the limit; critics ask why he has not personally restated his earlier rejection of third-term politics. CAJ also quoted the Law Association of Zambia's president, Arnold Kaluba: "The association maintains its position on presidential term limits and reiterates that the Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic". The agency's own framing was sharper, describing the August election as widely discredited by observers and the push as dividing the country; it quoted the analyst Brian Polombwe as saying the bid "is pouring fresh fuel onto an already toxic political atmosphere". CAJ put the youth consortium's expected turnout on 25 November at more than 60,000, a figure it gave as "reportedly expected" rather than confirmed.

body.text: An apology from an August ally

body: In a separate development reported only by the Zambian Observer among the outlets read for this story, the opposition leader Saviour Chishimba, who signs his statements Yehudah Ben David, issued a public apology on Wednesday 18 November to supporters disappointed by his decision to join the UPND Alliance and campaign for President Hichilema in August. "To everyone who felt disregarded, disappointed or betrayed, I tender my most sincere and unreserved apology," he wrote, in the text the Observer published. He said the decision was his own political judgment, shaped by his detention without trial between 2016 and 2021 and a wish to preserve economic stabilisation after Zambia's debt default; that he was offered no money or post; and that he had once given up a parliamentary seat three weeks before mid-term gratuities fell due. "My decision involved no pecuniary transaction," he said. The Observer did not say who had alleged otherwise, and carried no response from the UPND.

stories.title: US$105 million through Zanaco for small firms, and a K5 billion State guarantee scheme in the 2027 Budget: Katotobwe asks that the money reach businesses that can use it
stories.excerpt: Four development lenders and Citi have put together a US$105 million facility to be lent through Zanaco to small and medium-sized enterprises, with Swedfund and FinDev Canada providing US$35 million each, Norfund US$25 million and Citi US$10 million, Zambia Monitor and the pan-African outlet Afrimag reported after the signing in Lusaka on Wednesday 18 November. Trade and Exports Minister Caroline Katotobwe used the occasion to point to the 2027 Budget's K5 billion Small-Business Guarantee Scheme and a planned development finance institution.

image.label: US$105 million
image.caption: A syndicated facility led by Citi will be lent through Zanaco to small and medium-sized Zambian businesses, with a focus on women-led firms and agriculture.

body: Zambia's small businesses have a new line of credit and the promise of a State guarantee behind the next one. At a signing ceremony in Lusaka on Wednesday 18 November, Zanaco, Citi, FinDev Canada, Norfund and Swedfund concluded a US$105 million financing partnership for small and medium-sized enterprises, Zambia Monitor reported that evening. The money is split four ways: US$35 million each from Swedfund, Sweden's development finance institution, and FinDev Canada; US$25 million from Norway's Norfund; and US$10 million from Citi. It will be lent through Zanaco to eligible SMEs, with women-owned and women-led businesses and firms along the agricultural value chain among the stated targets.

Afrimag, a pan-African business outlet, reported the same facility on Wednesday as a syndicated loan led by Citibank and closed by Zanaco to widen access to credit for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. Its account adds that Swedfund's US$35 million carries a European Union guarantee under the MSME Platform Plus programme, part of the EU's Global Gateway initiative, and that this is Swedfund's second commitment in Zambia. Afrimag quotes Siongo Kisoso, Swedfund's regional director for East Africa, as saying that the need for long-term capital in Zambia's MSME sector is significant and that the facility is meant to reach underserved communities. Lusaka Brief could not read Swedfund's own release, which Afrimag cites, and the EU guarantee is reported on Afrimag's account alone.

body.text: The minister's ask, and the Budget's promise

body: Caroline Katotobwe, the Minister of Trade and Exports, told the signing that the Government welcomed the partnership and asked Zanaco to make sure the money reached viable Zambian businesses, Zambia Monitor reported. She said the aim was capital structured so that firms could expand production, buy machinery, improve quality, add value and meet domestic and export orders. "Our expectation is that this financing will translate into tangible outcomes", she said. She also pointed to what the State itself is putting on the table: "The 2027 National Budget recognises this need through initiatives such as the K5 billion Small-Business Guarantee Scheme", she said, adding that the Government plans a development finance institution to improve access to affordable business finance.

A K5 billion guarantee for small firms is not an entirely new idea. In October 2025, Zambia Monitor reported that the Bank of Zambia Governor, Denny Kalyalya, had told the 2026 budget symposium that the central bank would launch a K5 billion fund in the first quarter of 2026 to provide credit guarantees to SMEs, that 15 fund managers had applied to run it, and that the bank was setting up a special-purpose vehicle to hold it. Wednesday's report does not say whether the Budget's Small-Business Guarantee Scheme is that vehicle under a new name or a separate instrument, nor whether the Bank of Zambia fund was launched on schedule; Lusaka Brief has not found a report that settles either point.

The Canadian High Commission in Zambia, Swedfund and Norfund reaffirmed their support for Zambian SMEs and women entrepreneurs at the signing, Zambia Monitor said, without giving further figures. Katotobwe encouraged the firms that borrow to invest in innovation and productivity so that they can compete regionally and internationally.

stories.title: Seventy-one per cent of the market: Sialubalo orders a national crackdown on illicit alcohol, as Zambian Breweries links 43 per cent of Chainama admissions to illicit drink
stories.excerpt: Local Government Minister Gift Sialubalo has directed enforcement agencies to step up inspections of unlicensed liquor outlets, dismantle illegal manufacturing and distribution networks and tighten border surveillance, telling a liquor enforcement conference in Lusaka on Wednesday 18 November that illicit alcohol is estimated at 71 per cent of Zambia's market, Zambia Monitor and the Daily Nation report. Zambian Breweries' managing director said 43 per cent of psychiatric admissions at Chainama Hills Hospital were linked to high-strength illicit alcohol.

image.label: 71 per cent
image.caption: The Government estimates that illicit alcohol accounts for 71 per cent of Zambia's market and has ordered inspections, raids and border checks.

body: The Government has ordered a national crackdown on illicit alcohol, which it says makes up almost three-quarters of everything Zambians drink. Gift Sialubalo, the Minister of Local Government and Rural Development, issued the directive at the National Joint Stakeholders Liquor Enforcement Conference in Lusaka on Wednesday 18 November, Zambia Monitor reported that afternoon. He told enforcement agencies to step up inspections of unlicensed liquor outlets, dismantle illegal manufacturing and distribution networks and tighten surveillance at the borders. The Daily Nation reported the minister's pledge of tougher enforcement on Wednesday with the same estimate: that illicit alcohol accounts for 71 per cent of the country's market.

Sialubalo said the illicit trade threatens public health, undermines legitimate businesses and deprives the Treasury of tax revenue. The Government's plan, as both outlets describe it, is to strengthen liquor licensing, improve compliance monitoring and run joint enforcement operations, which the minister said would protect consumers, broaden the tax base, improve revenue collection and support the Grow Zambia Agenda. He said the fight required a coordinated response involving local authorities and other agencies. Neither report says who produced the 71 per cent estimate or how it was arrived at.

The sharpest numbers of the day came from the industry. Thais Cavinatto, managing director of Zambian Breweries, told the conference that consumption of illicit alcohol had risen by more than 22 percentage points over the past five years, Zambia Monitor reported, and warned that alcohol made without quality controls or safety standards carries significant health risks. She cited a figure that 43 per cent of patients admitted to psychiatric units at Chainama Hills Hospital were there because of harmful consumption of high-strength illicit alcohol, and said the trade threatens jobs, discourages investment and denies the Government billions of kwacha in tax. Those figures are the company's; Zambia Monitor's report does not say where they come from, and Chainama Hills Hospital has not been reported as commenting.

Lusaka's Town Clerk, Oliver Muuka, urged manufacturers and distributors to comply with the law and with quality standards for producing and selling alcoholic drinks, describing compliance as both a legal and a corporate responsibility. The 71 per cent figure is an estimate, and neither report explains how it was reached. No trader, brewer of traditional spirits or consumer group was reported as responding to the directive on Wednesday.

stories.title: Four deaths in a day and 82 new suspected cases: the cholera toll reaches 75 as the count passes 3,250, and Mpongwe opens a treatment centre with 26 patients
stories.excerpt: Zambia recorded 82 new suspected cholera cases and four deaths in 24 hours, News Diggers reported on Thursday 19 November, citing the Zambia National Public Health Institute: 3,258 suspected cases since the outbreak was declared on 28 July, 464 of them confirmed, 75 deaths, 98 patients in hospital and 3,085 discharged. Three days earlier Zambia Monitor had reported 3,099 cases, 68 deaths and 27 districts affected across seven provinces. On the Copperbelt, Mpongwe's district health director said a dedicated centre was treating 26 patients.

image.label: 75 deaths
image.caption: The cholera outbreak declared on 28 July has now killed 75 people, with 3,258 suspected cases recorded by 19 November.

body: The cholera outbreak declared on 28 July has entered its most lethal stretch in weeks. In the 24 hours to Thursday 19 November, the country recorded 82 new suspected cases and four deaths, News Diggers reported that morning, citing the Zambia National Public Health Institute (ZNPHI). Eighteen of the new cases have since been confirmed by laboratory. The cumulative count now stands at 3,258 suspected cases, of which 464 are confirmed; 75 people have died; 98 patients are in hospital; and 3,085 have recovered and been discharged. The figures beyond the opening paragraphs of the Diggers report sit behind that outlet's subscription.

The trend is clear when set against Zambia Monitor's report of Monday 16 November, based on the ZNPHI update of that day: 3,099 cumulative cases, 437 confirmed, 68 deaths, 101 patients under treatment and 2,930 discharged, with 74 new cases and two deaths in the preceding 24 hours. Between the two updates, three days apart, the case count rose by 159 and the death toll by seven. A week earlier still, on 12 November, Diggers had reported 2,658 suspected cases and 56 deaths.

Zambia Monitor's 16 November report listed 27 affected districts across seven provinces. Lusaka District accounted for 1,959 of the 3,099 cases, followed by Chibombo with 371, Chongwe 158, Chilanga 130, Mpulungu 90, Chiengi and Mwansabombwe 86 each, and Mpongwe 61. Smaller numbers were recorded in Nsama, Nchelenge, Mwense, Mumbwa, Monze, Kaputa, Pemba, Chisamba, Kafue, Kitwe, Shibuyunji, Mbala, Sinazongwe, Solwezi, Chikankata, Livingstone, Kalomo, Mazabuka and Ndola, the last three with a single case each. ZNPHI's advice, as the report carried it, was that anyone with watery diarrhoea or vomiting should go to the nearest health facility immediately, and that households should wash hands with soap, drink boiled or treated water, cook food thoroughly and use clean toilets.

On the Copperbelt, the picture in Mpongwe has changed within a week. On 12 November, Diggers reported that the provincial health director, Dr Charles Mwinuna, had refuted reports of two suspected cholera deaths in the district and said the province had recorded only three cases. By Thursday, the same outlet was quoting Mpongwe's district health director, Dr Evaristo Kunka, as saying the district had admitted 26 cholera patients at a dedicated treatment centre. "We have created a cholera centre and we have about 26 patients...", he said, in the extract available to non-subscribers.

When Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi gave Parliament a ministerial statement on Thursday 29 October, Zambia Monitor reported, the outbreak stood at 1,622 cases, 228 confirmed, and 30 deaths across 20 districts in six provinces; 16 of those deaths had occurred in communities before the patients reached a health facility. The minister told MPs that 709,018 people had received oral cholera vaccine, 91 per cent of the target population, out of 782,147 doses approved by the International Coordinating Group, and that the Treasury had released K13 million for emergency water supply. In the three weeks since, the case count has doubled and the death toll has risen two and a half times. No updated vaccination figure appears in this week's reports.

stories.title: A guard of honour and a goal inside a minute: ZESCO United send captain Lindo Mkhonta off with a 2–1 win over Red Arrows, as Napsa, Chirundu and Kabwe Warriors win late
stories.excerpt: Lindo Mkhonta's last match for ZESCO United ended in a 2–1 win over Red Arrows at Trade Fair Grounds in Ndola on Thursday 19 November, ZamFoot reported: Luka Mutoshi headed in inside the first minute, Kelvin Kampamba's cross went in off a defender in the 53rd, and Jonathan Manda replied for Arrows in the 71st. Elsewhere in matchweek eight of the MTN Super League transitional season, Napsa Stars beat Makeni All Stars 2–1 with a stoppage-time winner, Chirundu United won 1–0 at Roan United in the 92nd minute and Kabwe Warriors won 1–0 at Mufulira Wanderers.

image.label: Mkhonta's last match
image.caption: ZESCO United beat Red Arrows 2–1 in Ndola on Thursday in the farewell match of their Eswatini captain, Lindo Mkhonta.

body: Lindo Mkhonta's farewell went the way his team-mates had promised at breakfast. Before kick-off at Trade Fair Grounds in Ndola on Thursday 19 November, ZESCO United formed a guard of honour for their captain, an Eswatini defender who joined from Young Buffaloes in 2023 and who leaves at the end of the month to attend to personal and professional commitments at home, the club confirmed in a statement carried by ZamFoot. Within a minute of the start, Luka Mutoshi had headed in his first goal in ZESCO colours from a Rally Bwalya free kick and cross, beating Red Arrows goalkeeper Kenny Mumba, according to the club's own match report, which ZamFoot republished.

Coach Mwenya Chipepo made two changes at half-time, sending on Kelvin Kampamba for Bwalya and Elvis Addae for Yves Allarabaye. In the 53rd minute Kampamba's cross evaded everyone and went in after a slight touch off Arrows defender Brian Chilimina for 2–0. Jonathan Manda pulled one back for Arrows in the 71st minute, but ZESCO held on for their second home win of the campaign. Kampamba, the club report says, had told Mkhonta at breakfast that morning: "We are winning this one for you." The result leaves ZESCO second in Stream B on 13 points from eight matches, four behind leaders Green Eagles, who have a game in hand; Red Arrows are eighth with five points from five.

body.text: Four years, three goals and two trophies

body: Mkhonta rose to the captaincy during close to four years in Ndola and played in ZESCO's 2025 ABSA Cup win over Red Arrows and their Charity Shield victory against Power Dynamos, ZamFoot reported in a preview on Thursday morning. He scored three goals for the club, one in the league and two in the ABSA Cup. Kennedy Chiyombwe, ZESCO United's chief executive, said: "Lindo has been a dedicated player of Zesco United Football Club." The departing captain thanked the club and the people of Zambia: "My stay here has been a good one." Milton Syulikwa, a board member and the club's technical chairperson, paid tribute to his experience and leadership, ZamFoot said.

Four other fixtures were played on Thursday, ZamFoot reported. Napsa Stars beat Makeni All Stars 2–1 at home: Simon Nkhata scored in the 53rd minute, Kinsley Sakala equalised from a penalty in the 74th, and Leonard Lupiya won it four minutes into stoppage time. Napsa have seven points from eight matches, seventh in Stream A; Makeni are bottom with one point from seven. Chirundu United won 1–0 at Roan United through Joseph Chilimina's goal in the 92nd minute, moving to 11 points from seven and fourth in Stream B. Kabwe Warriors won 1–0 at Mufulira Wanderers, Timothy Sakala scoring in the 41st minute after an error by Wanderers goalkeeper Kabwe Mulenga; Warriors have nine points from six, Wanderers four from eight. Nkwazi and Mutondo Stars drew 0–0.

stories.title: Nigeria in March for the under-23s after a 4–0 comeback over DR Congo, and Denmark recall Nadia Nadim, 38, for the Copper Queens friendly in Esbjerg on 5 December
stories.excerpt: Zambia's under-23s will play Nigeria over two legs in March 2027 for a place at the Egypt 2027 U-23 Africa Cup of Nations, after Nigeria overturned a 2–0 first-leg deficit with a 4–0 win over DR Congo in Ikenne on Tuesday 17 November, ZamFoot reported. The tournament doubles as the road to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The Copper Queens, meanwhile, learned on Thursday that Denmark have recalled striker Nadia Nadim, 108 caps and 38 goals, for their friendly in Esbjerg on 5 December.

image.label: Nigeria, March 2027
image.caption: Zambia's under-23s meet Nigeria over two legs in March 2027 for a place at the U-23 Africa Cup of Nations in Egypt.

body: The opponent for Zambia's under-23s in the last round of qualifying is settled, and it is the one with the longer pedigree. Nigeria beat DR Congo 4–0 at Remo Stars Stadium in Ikenne on Tuesday 17 November to win the tie 4–2 on aggregate, ZamFoot reported on Wednesday, having lost the first leg 2–0 in Lubumbashi. Alex Owolayefe opened the scoring in the eighth minute from a rebound, Bright Edokpolor made it 2–0 in the 55th, the substitute Victor Samuel put Nigeria ahead on aggregate for the first time eight minutes later from an Edokpolor pass, and Abdulmuiz Adeleke added a late penalty.

Zambia reached the third and final round by beating Burkina Faso 1–0 in Lusaka to level their tie at 1–1 on aggregate and then winning 3–2 on penalties. The two-legged tie against Nigeria is scheduled for March 2027, with a place at the 2027 U-23 Africa Cup of Nations in Egypt at stake; that tournament in turn decides Africa's places in the men's football event at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Nigeria won Olympic gold at Atlanta in 1996 but missed both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, ZamFoot noted. Dates, venues and the order of the legs have not been reported.

The Copper Queens' next opponents named their squad on Thursday 19 November, and it includes a name they will know. Denmark coach Jakob Michelsen has recalled Nadia Nadim, 38, who has 108 caps and 38 goals and who announced her international retirement after the 2025 European Championship before telling Michelsen over the summer that she was available again, ZamFoot reported. "I thought a lot about my future this summer, but came to the conclusion that I'm not done with football at all," Nadim said, as ZamFoot reported. She won the Danish league and cup with HB Køge last season and finished as the A-League's leading scorer. Michelsen said she had consistently delivered strong performances in both the A-League and the Champions League.

The friendly is on Saturday 5 December in Esbjerg and is Denmark's last international of 2026. Michelsen named a 24-player squad that also includes Pernille Harder and Stine Ballisager of Bayern Munich, Nikoline Nielsen of Barcelona, Kathrine Kühl of Atlético Madrid and Cecilie Fløe of Wolfsburg. Part of the squad gathers in Helsingør on 25 November and the full senior squad assembles in Marbella, Spain, on 27 November. ZamFoot's report did not name Zambia's squad or say when the Copper Queens travel; the Football Association of Zambia had not published a squad by Thursday evening in the reports read for this story.

analysis.title: A copper correction is a budget question before it is a currency one
analysis.body: A 6 per cent day in copper is loud, but the number that matters for Zambia is quieter: where the price settles over the next quarter. Zambia's revenue plans were drawn up while copper was near the record highs it reached in September, and the kwacha's firmness this year has leaned on the metal. If Thursday's stabilisation holds and the price sits near US$12,500 a tonne, that is roughly where the year began, not a crisis. If XTB's next support near US$11,680 gives way, the arithmetic changes for royalties, which rise and fall with the price, and for the export receipts that supply the interbank market. Two things are worth separating. The first is the financial market, which is unwinding a bet on artificial intelligence and tariffs. The second is the physical market, where both commentaries say Chinese stocks are critically low and spot copper trades at a premium. The first can fall a long way without the second moving. What to watch: Friday's London close, any Bank of Zambia comment on the kwacha, and whether the Treasury's revenue assumptions for 2027 are revisited in Parliament's budget debate.

analysis.title: Today's ruling is about the door, not the room
analysis.body: Whatever Judge Geoffrey Mulenga decides at 09:30, nobody walks out of Mukobeko today. The question before him is narrow: whether the Lusaka High Court can hear a bail application in a sedition case that began in Solwezi and has since been transferred to the Lusaka Subordinate Court. The State's case is procedural and not trivial. Bail is ordinarily sought first where the case is, and the DPP argues that going straight to the High Court while the matter sat in another court duplicated proceedings. The defence answers that no bail application was ever made in Solwezi, so there is nothing to duplicate, and that section 123 of the Criminal Procedure Code gives the High Court the power it needs. If the objection is upheld, the two men start again before a magistrate; if it is dismissed, the bail hearing itself proceeds, and the State can still oppose bail on the merits. Either way, the larger decision comes on Tuesday, when three judges rule on constitutional bail for all 18 treason accused, a charge the law ordinarily treats as non-bailable. The reasoning in both rulings will be read closely abroad, after Amnesty International's appeal this week.

analysis.title: The term-limits fight is moving from slogans to procedure
analysis.body: For a fortnight the argument over presidential term limits was conducted in statements. This week it shifted to rules, which is usually where constitutional disputes are decided. Three procedural questions are now open. First, the police: having advised two consortiums not to march on 25 November, they have been asked in writing for specific reasons and an alternative, with a hint of litigation if none comes. Public-order law in Zambia has been tested in court before, and a bare citation of intelligence may not satisfy a judge. Second, the Speaker: William Harrington's argument that Nelly Mutti should not preside, because she sat on the Mung'omba commission that rejected a third term, is a recusal claim of a kind Parliament rarely entertains, but it forces the House to say how a petition to change Article 106 would be handled. Third, the executive's distance: Jack Mwiimbu's line that the executive will not involve itself in the legislature's processes is consistent, and its critics' reply is that silence from the President is itself a position. What to watch is whether any of the three produces a document, a police reply, a Speaker's ruling or a State House statement, before Wednesday.
